# Decoder

[[Decoder]] is the output-generating half of [[Transformer Architecture]]. It predicts target tokens autoregressively, using previous target tokens and the contextual source representation from [[Encoder]].

Each decoder layer contains three sublayers: [[Masked Self-Attention]], [[Encoder-Decoder Attention]], and [[Feed Forward Network]]. These are wrapped with [[Residual Connection]] and [[Layer Normalization]].

## Why masking is needed

During training, the full target sentence is available. [[Masked Self-Attention]] prevents a position from seeing future target tokens, preserving the causal generation constraint.

## Source conditioning

[[Encoder-Decoder Attention]] lets the decoder query encoder outputs. This is how generated target tokens stay aligned with the source sequence.

# Encoder-Decoder Attention

[[Encoder-Decoder Attention]] connects the [[Decoder]] to the [[Encoder]]. The decoder provides queries, while the encoder outputs provide keys and values.

This mechanism lets each target position select relevant source positions. In machine translation, it plays the alignment role that earlier sequence-to-sequence models handled with attention over recurrent states.

## Difference from self-attention

[[Self-Attention]] relates tokens within the same sequence. Encoder-decoder attention relates target-side decoder states to source-side encoder states.

## Role in Transformer

Without this bridge, the decoder would only model the target prefix. With encoder-decoder attention, generation is conditioned on the input sentence.

# Encoder

[[Encoder]] is the input-processing half of [[Transformer Architecture]]. It transforms source tokens into contextual representations that the [[Decoder]] can consume through [[Encoder-Decoder Attention]].

Each encoder layer contains [[Multi-Head Attention]] applied as bidirectional [[Self-Attention]], followed by a [[Feed Forward Network]]. Each sublayer is wrapped with [[Residual Connection]] and [[Layer Normalization]].

## Information flow

[[Token Embedding]] and [[Positional Encoding]] create the initial sequence representation. The encoder then repeatedly mixes information across tokens with self-attention and transforms each position with a feed-forward network.

## Why it matters

The encoder is where the source sequence becomes a set of contextual token vectors. Unlike an RNN, all positions can be processed in parallel within each layer.

nodes.name: Feed Forward Network

# Feed Forward Network

[[Feed Forward Network]] is the position-wise MLP sublayer in each [[Encoder]] and [[Decoder]] layer. It applies the same two-layer neural network independently to every token position.

Attention mixes information across positions. The feed-forward network transforms each token representation after that mixing. This separation is important: attention handles communication, while the feed-forward network handles per-token nonlinear transformation.

## Role in Transformer

Each Transformer layer alternates global interaction through [[Multi-Head Attention]] with local transformation through the feed-forward network.

## Related concepts

- [[Residual Connection]] wraps the feed-forward sublayer.
- [[Layer Normalization]] stabilizes the output.

# Layer Normalization

[[Layer Normalization]] stabilizes activations inside [[Transformer Architecture]]. It normalizes features within each token representation and is paired with [[Residual Connection]] around each sublayer.

In the original paper, layer normalization is applied after the residual addition. Later variants often use pre-normalization to improve training stability in very deep Transformers.

## Role in Transformer

Layer normalization appears after attention and feed-forward sublayers in both [[Encoder]] and [[Decoder]].

## Related concepts

- [[Residual Connection]] preserves information flow.
- [[Feed Forward Network]] and attention sublayers rely on normalization for stable stacking.

# Limitations

[[Limitations]] captures the main tradeoffs of [[Transformer Architecture]]. The most important limitation is the O(n²) cost of [[Self-Attention]] with respect to sequence length. Every token can attend to every other token, which creates a full attention matrix.

Other limitations include weak built-in sequence bias compared with recurrence, sensitivity to positional representation, and interpretability risk when treating attention maps as explanations.

## Long-context cost

The quadratic attention matrix becomes expensive for long documents, high-resolution visual tokens, or long-context language modeling. This motivates sparse attention, linear attention, memory mechanisms, and retrieval-augmented systems.

## Related concepts

- [[Positional Encoding]] is necessary but not the final answer to sequence order.
- [[Multi-Head Attention]] produces visualizable weights, but attention visualization is not full causal explanation.

# Masked Self-Attention

[[Masked Self-Attention]] is [[Self-Attention]] with a causal mask. It is used inside the [[Decoder]] so each target position can attend only to earlier target positions and itself.

The mask is applied before softmax in [[Scaled Dot-Product Attention]]. Future positions receive impossible scores, so their attention weights become zero.

## Role in generation

This mechanism makes parallel training possible while preserving autoregressive behavior. At inference time, tokens are still generated step by step, but the training objective can use all target positions at once with the correct mask.

## Related concepts

- [[Decoder]] depends on masked self-attention.
- [[Encoder]] does not use causal masking because the source sequence is fully visible.

# Multi-Head Attention

[[Multi-Head Attention]] runs several attention heads in parallel. Each head has its own learned projections for queries, keys, and values, so different heads can attend to different relation types or representation subspaces.

This solves a limitation of a single attention operation: one attention distribution gives one weighted mixture per token. Multiple heads let the model combine several views, such as local syntax, long-distance dependency, positional relation, and semantic alignment.

## Role in Transformer

- [[Encoder]] uses multi-head self-attention.
- [[Decoder]] uses multi-head [[Masked Self-Attention]].
- [[Encoder-Decoder Attention]] is also implemented as multi-head attention.

## Interpretability caveat

Attention visualizations can reveal useful patterns, but attention weights should not be treated as a complete explanation of model reasoning.

# Positional Encoding

[[Positional Encoding]] injects order information into [[Transformer Architecture]]. Because [[Self-Attention]] is permutation-invariant by itself, the model needs an explicit signal that distinguishes first token, second token, and so on.

The original paper uses sinusoidal position vectors added to [[Token Embedding]]. Sine and cosine waves at different frequencies allow the model to represent absolute and relative positional patterns.

## Why it matters

Without positional encoding, the same set of tokens in a different order would look too similar to the attention mechanism. Position encoding makes sequence order available while preserving parallel computation.

## Later developments

The original sinusoidal encoding has limitations. Later models often use learned positional embeddings, relative position bias, RoPE, or ALiBi.

# Residual Connection

[[Residual Connection]] adds a sublayer input back to its output. In [[Transformer Architecture]], every attention and feed-forward sublayer is wrapped with a residual path and [[Layer Normalization]].

Residual paths help optimization because gradients can flow through shorter routes. They also let each layer refine a representation instead of replacing it completely.

## Role in Transformer

Residual connections appear around [[Multi-Head Attention]], [[Masked Self-Attention]], [[Encoder-Decoder Attention]], and [[Feed Forward Network]].

## Why it matters

Deep stacks of attention layers would be harder to train without residual structure. The residual path is part of why Transformer layers can be composed repeatedly.

# Scaled Dot-Product Attention

[[Scaled Dot-Product Attention]] is the primitive operation used by [[Self-Attention]] and [[Multi-Head Attention]]. It compares queries and keys with a dot product, divides by the square root of the key dimension, applies softmax, and uses the result to mix values.

The scaling factor stabilizes gradients when key/query dimensions are large. Without scaling, dot products can grow large, pushing softmax into regions with very small gradients.

## Formula

Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k)) V

## Related concepts

- [[Self-Attention]] applies this operation within one sequence.
- [[Encoder-Decoder Attention]] applies it from decoder queries to encoder keys and values.
- [[Masked Self-Attention]] adds a causal mask before softmax.

# Self-Attention

[[Self-Attention]] computes relationships among tokens inside the same sequence. Each token is projected into a query, key, and value. The query of one token is compared with keys from all tokens, producing weights over the corresponding values.

Self-attention is the mechanism that lets [[Transformer Architecture]] avoid recurrence. Any token can directly attend to any other token, so the path length between positions is constant rather than proportional to sequence distance.

## Role in Transformer

- In [[Encoder]], self-attention is bidirectional over the input sequence.
- In [[Decoder]], [[Masked Self-Attention]] restricts access to future tokens.
- [[Multi-Head Attention]] runs self-attention several times in parallel.

## Tradeoff

Self-attention is highly parallel, but the attention matrix scales as O(n²) with sequence length. This motivates later sparse and linear attention variants.

# Token Embedding

[[Token Embedding]] maps discrete token IDs into dense vectors. In [[Transformer Architecture]], token embeddings are the starting representation before [[Positional Encoding]] is added.

The embedding gives each token a learned semantic representation, while positional encoding gives it an order signal. Their sum becomes the input to the first [[Encoder]] or [[Decoder]] layer.

## Role in Transformer

Embeddings are shared conceptually across the model input and output vocabulary. The original paper also scales embeddings by the square root of the model dimension.

## Related concepts

- [[Positional Encoding]] complements token identity with order.
- [[Self-Attention]] uses the resulting vectors to build query, key, and value projections.

# Training and Results

[[Training and Results]] summarizes the empirical evidence for [[Transformer Architecture]]. The original paper reports strong machine translation performance on WMT 2014 English-German and English-French benchmarks.

The important result is not only better BLEU. The model trains much faster than recurrent alternatives because [[Self-Attention]] avoids sequential hidden-state computation and exposes more parallelism to GPUs.

## Reported outcomes

- Transformer base reaches strong translation quality with lower training cost.
- Transformer big improves quality further.
- The architecture generalizes beyond machine translation and later becomes the basis for BERT, GPT, T5, and many multimodal models.

## Related concepts

- [[Limitations]] explains why quadratic attention becomes a bottleneck for long contexts.
- [[Transformer Reading Path]] gives a learning order for the architecture.

# Transformer Architecture

[[Transformer Architecture]] is an encoder-decoder sequence model built around [[Self-Attention]] instead of recurrence or convolution. Its core design goal is to model token-to-token dependencies while allowing parallel computation across positions.

The architecture has two main halves: [[Encoder]] and [[Decoder]]. Both use [[Token Embedding]], [[Positional Encoding]], [[Residual Connection]], [[Layer Normalization]], and [[Feed Forward Network]]. The decoder additionally uses [[Masked Self-Attention]] and [[Encoder-Decoder Attention]] to generate output tokens autoregressively.

## Why it matters

The key claim is that attention alone is enough for high-quality sequence transduction. This makes long-range dependency paths short and makes training much more parallel than RNN-based models.

## Related concepts

- [[Self-Attention]] provides global token interaction.
- [[Multi-Head Attention]] expands attention into multiple learned relation subspaces.
- [[Training and Results]] gives empirical evidence for the design.
- [[Limitations]] explains the quadratic sequence-length cost.

# Transformer Reading Path

[[Transformer Reading Path]] gives a practical order for understanding [[Transformer Architecture]]. The goal is to move from the full model to the mechanisms that make it work.

## Recommended order

1. Start with [[Transformer Architecture]] to understand the whole encoder-decoder design.
2. Read [[Token Embedding]] and [[Positional Encoding]] to understand input representation.
3. Read [[Scaled Dot-Product Attention]] and [[Self-Attention]] to understand the core operation.
4. Read [[Multi-Head Attention]] to understand why multiple attention subspaces matter.
5. Read [[Encoder]] and [[Decoder]] to understand how layers are assembled.
6. Read [[Masked Self-Attention]] and [[Encoder-Decoder Attention]] to understand generation.
7. Read [[Residual Connection]], [[Layer Normalization]], and [[Feed Forward Network]] to understand trainable depth.
8. Finish with [[Training and Results]] and [[Limitations]].

## How to use with Understand-Anything

Generate the graph, open the dashboard, then follow this path as a guided conceptual tour. Use search for terms like attention, masking, position, residual, and long context.

knowledgeMeta.content:
# Attention Is All You Need

Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762

The paper introduces the Transformer, an encoder-decoder architecture based entirely on attention mechanisms. It removes recurrence and convolution from sequence transduction. The main mechanism is scaled dot-product attention, where each token produces query, key, and value vectors. Self-attention lets every token attend to every other token in the same sequence. Multi-head attention runs several attention operations in parallel so the model can represent different relation types in different subspaces.

The architecture uses token embeddings, sinusoidal positional encoding, residual connections, layer normalization, and position-wise feed-forward networks. The encoder stacks repeated layers containing self-attention and feed-forward sublayers. The decoder stacks repeated layers containing masked self-attention, encoder-decoder attention, and feed-forward sublayers.

The paper reports strong machine translation results on WMT 2014 English-German and English-French benchmarks, with faster training than recurrent or convolutional alternatives. Its key tradeoff is that self-attention has quadratic cost in sequence length, which is expensive for long contexts.
